## Blog

### Why a weekly design sprint beats a three-month contract

Source: https://vino-costa.com/blog/weekly-design-sprint/

How short cycles turn an idea into investor-ready UI without a black box in the middle.

Most design contracts fail the same way: a long brief, weeks of silence, and a big reveal that misses the mark. A weekly sprint removes the silence — you see the work while it is still cheap to change.

#### What a week actually contains

Monday is the brief and the moodboard. Tuesday maps flows. Wednesday brings two or three concepts of the key screen. Thursday folds in your comments. Friday hands off files, a design system and a short report.

- you approve direction on day three, not month three
- every step leaves an artifact you can show your team
- the scope for the next week is picked from what you learned in this one

#### When it does not fit

If the product needs months of research before a single screen makes sense, a sprint is the wrong tool. Sprints work when there is a concrete flow to ship — onboarding, a dashboard, a landing.

---

### How a UX audit boosts conversion

Source: https://vino-costa.com/blog/ux-audit-conversion/

What I check in an express interface audit and why it pays off faster than a redesign.

An audit costs less than a redesign and almost always comes first: it shows what to fix and stops you rebuilding what already works.

#### What I look at first

The path to the target action, form friction, readability of the key numbers, and behaviour on a phone. Then the gaps between what the landing promises and what the product actually shows.

- how many steps to the first useful action
- where attention drops: long forms, unclear buttons, extra fields
- whether the promise at the entrance matches the interface inside

#### What you get

A prioritized report: fix now, fix later, leave alone. Each item comes with a plain reason and an effort estimate.

> An audit isn't about taste. It's about where people leave and what stops them.

---

### RWA on-chain: a rental design case

Source: https://vino-costa.com/blog/rwa-onchain-case/

UX/UI for tokenizing real-world assets — a breakdown from structure to the deal screen.

Tokenizing real-world assets doesn't stall on the blockchain — it stalls on trust: people need to understand what exactly they own.

#### The problem

Show a share in a property so it reads without a glossary: what was bought, what it earns, when and how to exit.

#### The solution

An asset card with three numbers instead of ten, a payout calendar and a predictable exit path. Complexity moves into disclosure blocks so the first screen doesn't scare anyone off.

- structure: property → share → income → exit
- numbers large, terms next to them, fine print gone
- deal states readable without contacting support

---

### Kaizen in design: continuous improvement

Source: https://vino-costa.com/blog/kaizen-in-design/

How a method of small constant improvements is built into the weekly sprint.

A big once-a-year redesign almost always misses: by the time it ships, the product has moved on.

#### Small steps instead of one big leap

One measurable improvement a week: a screen, a flow, a component. The change ships, you watch the numbers, the next week is planned on the result.

#### Why it works

- a mistake costs a week, not a quarter
- the team sees movement instead of waiting for the big reveal
- the design system grows alongside the work, not as a separate project
